issues.legal_issue: Trees attached to acquired land form part of the land for determining market value, and their assessed value attracts the statutory additional allowance.
material_facts: The acquired property included an orchard with trees standing on the land.
The value of the trees was determined to fix the market value of the acquired land.
The High Court treated the tree value as falling under a separate compensation head and disallowed the additional allowance on it.
issues.conclusion: The trees were components of the acquired land, and the additional allowance under section 23(2) had to be applied to the determined value of the land, including the value attributed to the trees.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(a) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, land includes benefits arising from land and things attached to the earth. Section 23(1) provides for determining the market value of the acquired land, and section 23(2) requires the statutory additional allowance on that value. The Court approved Sub-Collector of Godavari v. Seragam Subbareyadu and Krishna Bai v. The Secretary of State for India in Council, which treated trees standing on acquired land as included in the land’s market value for this purpose.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.trees_attached_to_acquired_land: Trees were standing on and attached to the acquired land.
predicates.tree_value_used_to_determine_land_market: The value attributed to the trees was used to determine the market value of the acquired land.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns compensation for land with attached trees whose value was used to determine the land’s market value, the additional allowance applies to that tree value.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not rely on fresh documents considered outside the record without admitting them as evidence and giving the opposing party an opportunity to rebut them.
material_facts: The High Court considered documents that were not part of the record.
The documents were considered after the arguments had concluded.
The appellants were not given an opportunity to rebut conclusions drawn from those documents.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have relied on the documents; they were excluded from consideration, although their exclusion did not assist the appellants in the result.
issues.legal_principle: If a court wishes to take fresh evidence into consideration, it must admit that evidence in accordance with law and give the opposing party an opportunity to rebut it. No earlier case or statutory provision was cited for this conclusion.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and fresh_documents_considered and documents_not_admitted_as_evidence and opposing_party_denied_chance_to_rebut

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The matter is being considered by an appellate court.
predicates.fresh_documents_considered: The court considered documents that had not previously formed part of the record.
predicates.documents_not_admitted_as_evidence: The documents were not admitted as evidence in accordance with law.
predicates.opposing_party_denied_chance_to_rebut: The opposing party was not given an opportunity to answer or rebut the documents.

issues.definition: In an appeal, fresh documents that were considered without lawful admission and without an opportunity for the opposing party to rebut them are excluded from consideration.

issues.legal_issue: A fact-finder assessing compensation is not bound to accept oral evidence merely because it was not effectively challenged or contradicted by rebuttal evidence.
material_facts: The appellants relied on oral testimony to support their claimed value for the orchard.
The appellants produced no documentary evidence supporting that claim.
The witnesses were not effectively cross-examined, and the Collector adduced no evidence in rebuttal.
The High Court found the oral evidence unacceptable after assessing it in light of probabilities and experience.
issues.conclusion: The court was not bound to accept the appellants’ oral evidence and could reject it as unacceptable.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing the value of oral evidence, judges may use their experience of life and test the evidence against probabilities; they are not bound to accept testimony simply because it was not effectively cross-examined or contradicted by rebuttal evidence. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.

rule.if: compensation_assessment_appeal and claim_supported_by_oral_testimony and no_documentary_support and fact_finder_assesses_evidence_on_probabilities

predicates.compensation_assessment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which compensation is being assessed.
predicates.claim_supported_by_oral_testimony: The claimant relied on oral testimony to support the claimed compensation.
predicates.no_documentary_support: The claimant supplied no documentary evidence supporting the claim.
predicates.fact_finder_assesses_evidence_on_probabi: The fact-finder assessed the testimony against probabilities and its experience of life.

issues.definition: In an appeal assessing compensation, when a claim rests on oral testimony without documentary support and the fact-finder tests it against probabilities, the fact-finder is not bound to accept that testimony.

issues.legal_issue: An enhanced compensation valuation is not disturbed in favour of a claimant where the claimant’s supporting evidence is rejected, the valuation remains above the original award, and the respondent has not appealed.
material_facts: The original compensation award was increased by the District Court.
The High Court reduced the District Court’s award but left the compensation above the original award.
The High Court’s valuation relied on documents that should have been excluded.
The High Court rejected the appellants’ oral evidence supporting their higher claim.
The Government did not appeal against the High Court’s decision.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not obtain further assistance from the exclusion of the documents, and the High Court’s enhanced valuation stood because the Government had not appealed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reasoned that, once the appellants’ evidence was rejected, the original award would have remained; the High Court had nevertheless enhanced that award, and the Government had not appealed. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_appeal_by_claimant and claimant_supporting_evidence_rejected and valuation_remains_above_original_award and respondent_did_not_appeal

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal_by_: The proceeding is a land-acquisition compensation appeal brought by the claimant seeking a further increase.
predicates.claimant_supporting_evidence_rejected: The court rejected the claimant’s evidence supporting the higher compensation claim.
predicates.valuation_remains_above_original_award: The valuation under appeal remains higher than the original compensation award.
predicates.respondent_did_not_appeal: The respondent did not appeal against the enhanced valuation.

issues.definition: When a claimant’s compensation appeal challenges a valuation above the original award, the claimant’s supporting evidence has been rejected, and the respondent has not appealed, the enhanced valuation is left undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: The award of costs is a matter of judicial discretion, and an appellate court need not interfere with a reasoned costs order where the claim was exaggerated and most supporting evidence was unacceptable.
material_facts: The lower courts directed the parties to bear their own costs.
The appellants’ compensation claim was found to be highly exaggerated.
Most of the evidence adduced by the appellants was found unacceptable.
The lower courts gave reasons for their costs orders.
issues.conclusion: There was no reason to interfere with the orders directing the parties to bear their own costs.
issues.legal_principle: Costs are essentially in the discretion of the courts. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_costs_order and lower_court_exercised_costs_discretion and claim_found_exaggerated and most_supporting_evidence_found_unacceptable and costs_order_supported_by_reasons

predicates.appeal_challenging_costs_order: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a costs order.
predicates.lower_court_exercised_costs_discretion: The lower court made the costs order as an exercise of its discretion.
predicates.claim_found_exaggerated: The claimant’s claim was found to be exaggerated.
predicates.most_supporting_evidence_found_unaccepta: Most of the evidence offered in support of the claim was found unacceptable.
predicates.costs_order_supported_by_reasons: The lower court gave reasons for its costs order.

issues.definition: In an appeal challenging a reasoned discretionary costs order, where the claim was found exaggerated and most supporting evidence unacceptable, the costs order is not disturbed.
